prompt: Why can one copy of a model's weights in GPU memory serve many users at once?

options.A: Weights are recomputed for every request
options.B: At inference the weights are only read, never written; each request's activations are separate and temporary
options.C: Users take turns, one request at a time
options.D: Each user gets a private copy of the weights

prompt: Who decides a token's query, and how does it get good at finding useful words?

options.A: A learned matrix W_Q multiplies the token's vector; training adjusts W_Q whenever a better query would have lowered the loss
options.B: It is drawn at random for each request
options.C: The tokenizer assigns a query to each token ID
options.D: Engineers write rules for what each word should look for

prompt: Blend two values with a weighted average: 4 with share 75%, 8 with share 25%.
Why run several attention heads instead of one, at the same total width?

options.A: Heads run on different layers
options.B: More heads means more parameters
options.C: Each head has its own softmax, so it can focus sharply on its own target (one on “river” for meaning, another on the previous word for grammar); one softmax would blur all needs into one average
options.D: Heads are spare copies for fault tolerance

prompt: Why can't an LLM reliably count the r's in “strawberry”?

options.A: The word was rare in its training data
options.B: It receives a few opaque token IDs (like str + aw + berry); the letters inside each piece are not part of its input
options.C: Softmax rounds small counts to zero
options.D: Temperature adds randomness to counting

prompt: A model writes a 100-token answer. Roughly how many times does the whole model run?

options.A: Once per sentence in the answer
options.B: Once per layer, so 32 times for a 32-layer model
options.C: About 100 times: one pass per new token, each pass with the previous token appended
options.D: Once: one pass produces the whole answer

prompt: Why does it help that similar words have nearby rows?

options.A: It lets the tokenizer merge synonyms into one token
options.B: Nearby rows share storage, so the model is smaller
options.C: Everything after the embedding is smooth math, so similar inputs give similar outputs: what was learned from “the river flooded” carries over to “the stream flooded”
options.D: The model looks up the nearest training sentence

prompt: What does a gradient tell training?

options.A: For each number, how much the error would change if that number moved a little, so training can step each one the way that lowers the error
options.B: Which neuron fired the most
options.C: How big a step to take (the learning rate)
options.D: The correct next token at each position

prompt: The same paragraph costs more tokens in Hindi than in English. Why can't fine-tuning the model fix this?

options.A: Hindi needs more weights, and fine-tuning can't add weights
options.B: The tokenizer is trained once, before the model, and then frozen; training the model never changes how text is split
options.C: Fine-tuning could fix it, but it is too expensive to bother
options.D: Providers bill per word, not per token

prompt: “The river bank flooded” and “The bank raised rates”. Compare the row looked up for “bank” in the two sentences.

options.A: The same row, but the model edits it for the second sentence
options.B: Different rows: the tokenizer picks the meaning from context
options.C: Identical: the same ID reads the same row; context is mixed in later by attention
options.D: Different rows, because their positions differ

prompt: How does “an LLM is a function, not a lookup table” explain hallucination?

options.A: It computes a plausible next token for any input from learned patterns; nothing checks that a source for the claim exists
options.B: It retrieves the nearest stored document and sometimes retrieves the wrong one
options.C: Hallucination comes only from sampling randomness; at temperature 0 it can't happen
options.D: The fact's token is missing from the vocabulary, so a similar token is substituted

prompt: An embedding table has one row per vocabulary token. Vocabulary 100,000, width 4,096. How many learned numbers are in the table, in millions?
Why can't a token ID be fed to the model as a plain number?

options.A: IDs change from one request to the next
options.B: The model only accepts decimals between 0 and 1
options.C: IDs are too large for a GPU to handle
options.D: IDs are arbitrary labels: ID 500 is not “close to” 501 in meaning, so arithmetic on them is meaningless. Each ID selects a learned row (a vector) instead

prompt: Which of these are learned weights (changed only by training), not per-request activations? Pick all that apply.

options.A: The output table used to score the next token
options.B: The attention weights (softmax shares) for this sentence
options.C: The embedding table
options.D: The query, key and value matrices (W_Q, W_K, W_V)
options.E: “bank”'s blended vector after attention in this sentence

prompt: “bank” is used in water sentences and in money sentences. Where does its embedding row end up?

options.A: Two separate rows, one per meaning
options.B: Somewhere between the water and money clusters; attention picks the meaning later from context
options.C: At random, because ambiguous words get no training signal
options.D: In the water cluster, because the first meaning seen wins

prompt: Remove all position information. What happens to “dog bites man” versus “man bites dog”?

options.A: Only the last word's meaning is lost
options.B: The tokenizer reorders the words alphabetically
options.C: Attention receives the same set of vectors either way, so it can't tell the two orders apart
options.D: The model crashes on repeated words

prompt: Which of these tasks are hard for an LLM for the same reason as counting letters? Pick all that apply.

options.A: Translating a common sentence
options.B: Exact arithmetic on long numbers
options.C: Reversing a word letter by letter
options.D: Finding words that rhyme

prompt: Why do LLMs split text into subword pieces rather than single characters?

options.A: Characters can't represent languages other than English
options.B: A character vocabulary would be too large to store
options.C: Characters make sequences several times longer, and attention's work grows with the square of the length
options.D: A model can't learn spelling from characters

prompt: Context grows from 8,000 to 32,000 tokens. By what factor does the number of attention scores grow?
Compare softmax([3, 1]) with softmax([2, 0]).

options.A: The first gives a flatter distribution
options.B: Identical: softmax depends only on the gaps between scores
options.C: The first gives the top score a bigger share, because its scores are larger
options.D: They can't be compared without knowing the vocabulary

prompt: Compute the dot product of [2, 1, 0] and [1, 3, 5].
Softmax of the scores [2, 0]. What share does the first score get, in percent? (e ≈ 2.718)
In “The river bank flooded”, which words can “bank” attend to?

options.A: All four words
options.B: Only “river”
options.C: Only “flooded”
options.D: “The”, “river”, and “bank” itself

prompt: How does byte-pair encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary?

options.A: Learn the pieces by gradient descent while the model trains
options.B: Start from single bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent neighbouring pair into a new token
options.C: Linguists write a list of prefixes and suffixes
options.D: Split at spaces and keep the most common words

prompt: Why must the attention shares add up to 100%?

options.A: So they can be read as probabilities of the next token
options.B: So that negative scores cancel out positive ones
options.C: The next step is a weighted average; shares summing to 1 keep the blend on the same scale as the inputs, whatever the number of words
options.D: GPUs require normalized numbers

prompt: A tokenizer has no single piece for four spaces. What happens when you send it Python code indented with four spaces?

options.A: The spaces are dropped, so the code reaches the model broken
options.B: Nothing: whitespace is free
options.C: Each indent becomes several tokens, so the same code costs more and fills the context window sooner
options.D: The model refuses the input

prompt: Why don't LLMs use whole words as tokens?

options.A: Whole words make sequences too long
options.B: Whole words can't be turned into vectors
options.C: Attention can only compare pieces shorter than a word
options.D: The vocabulary would need millions of entries and would still fail on any unseen word: a new name, a typo, a code identifier

prompt: Put one attention step for “bank” in the right order.

options.A: query · each value → softmax → weighted average of the keys
options.B: softmax of the values → dot with each key → add the query
options.C: weighted average of the keys, using the query as the shares
options.D: query · each key → divide by √(head size) → softmax → weighted average of the values

prompt: Why use three separate vectors (query, key, value) instead of the token's embedding for everything?

options.A: One vector is needed per attention head
options.B: To triple the model's memory for facts
options.C: What a word looks for, what it matches on, and what it hands over are different jobs; separate learned matrices let each be tuned on its own
options.D: Embeddings can't be multiplied together

prompt: Which backend operation has the same cost shape as attention over n tokens?

options.A: A single sequential scan: n
options.B: A self-join comparing every row with every earlier row: about n²/2
options.C: A B-tree index lookup: log n
options.D: A hash lookup: constant time

prompt: The score for “flooded” is bank's row · flooded's output row. After one training step, one column of bank's row moved a lot and another didn't move at all. Why?

options.A: The column that didn't move had already reached its final value
options.B: Columns are updated at random
options.C: Each column's nudge is proportional to the matching column of the other vector in the dot product; where that column is near zero, it barely affects the score, so its gradient is near zero
options.D: Only the first column of each row is trainable

prompt: A model learns positions as a second table with one row per slot (slots 1 to 4,096). What does that design imply?

options.A: A hard length limit: there is no row for slot 4,097
options.B: The vocabulary must also have 4,096 tokens
options.C: Word order no longer matters
options.D: Positions keep updating during inference

prompt: Every token scores itself and every earlier token: n(n+1)/2 scores. How many scores for 4,000 tokens (per head, per layer)?
A model is 4,096 numbers wide and runs 32 attention heads. How many numbers wide is each head?
A language needs 3× as many tokens for the same meaning. What follows? Pick all that apply.

options.A: Less text fits in the context window
options.B: The model has more weights for that language
options.C: Higher cost per request (billed per token)
options.D: Prefill gets faster

prompt: Nobody labels “river” and “stream” as related. How do their embedding rows end up close?

options.A: Attention copies one row into the other at inference time
options.B: A dictionary of synonyms is loaded before training
options.C: They appear in similar sentences (“the ___ overflowed”), so training's corrections nudge their rows in similar directions
options.D: The tokenizer gives them neighbouring IDs
